summaries.core-syntax: Names, assignment, operators, unpacking, and the small pieces of syntax used throughout Python.
summaries.control-flow: Choose what runs, repeat work, and control whether a loop stops, skips, or continues.
summaries.strings: Create, inspect, split, combine, search, format, encode, and transform text.
summaries.numbers: Work with integers, floating-point values, precise decimals, fractions, and common math operations.
summaries.collections: Store groups of values using lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries, each with different behavior.
summaries.comprehensions: Build collections or lazy generators compactly from other iterables, optionally filtering values.
summaries.functions: Define reusable behavior, control how arguments are accepted, and understand how names are resolved.
summaries.iterators-generators: Understand Python's iteration protocol and produce values lazily instead of building everything at once.
summaries.exceptions: Represent failures explicitly, catch only expected errors, and guarantee cleanup when execution leaves a block.
summaries.oop: Model state and behavior with classes, instances, inheritance, properties, and alternative constructors.
summaries.dataclasses-enum: Reduce class boilerplate for data objects and represent a fixed set of named values.
summaries.dunder-methods: Hook your objects into Python syntax such as printing, comparison, iteration, indexing, and context managers.
summaries.typing: Describe expected value shapes for editors, static type checkers, documentation, and safer refactoring.
summaries.modules-imports: Split code into modules and packages, import public names, and control module execution.
summaries.files-pathlib: Read, write, locate, create, rename, and inspect files and directories safely.
summaries.data-formats: Convert Python values to and from common text or binary formats such as JSON, CSV, TOML, and Base64.
summaries.datetime: Represent dates, times, durations, timestamps, and time zones without losing temporal context.
summaries.stdlib-toolbox: Useful batteries-included data structures and algorithms that often replace custom utility code.
summaries.os-cli: Interact with the operating system, environment variables, command-line arguments, subprocesses, and temporary files.
summaries.logging-debugging: Observe what a program is doing, inspect failures, stop execution interactively, and measure small code paths.
summaries.concurrency: Choose between synchronous code, async I/O, threads, and processes based on what is waiting or consuming CPU.
summaries.testing: Express expected behavior, isolate dependencies, prepare reusable test data, and run focused automated checks.
summaries.sqlite: Use Python's built-in SQLite driver for lightweight relational storage, queries, parameters, and transactions.
summaries.internals-gotchas: Common Python behaviors that cause subtle bugs when object identity, mutation, copying, or evaluation is misunderstood.

core-syntax.print: Send a human-readable representation of values to standard output.
core-syntax.assign: Bind a name to an object. Assignment does not copy the object.
core-syntax.multiple assign: Bind several names from several values in one statement by unpacking them.
core-syntax.swap: Exchange two bindings without a temporary variable.
core-syntax.augmented: Update a binding using an operation such as addition or multiplication; mutability affects whether the object itself changes.
core-syntax.membership: Check whether a value is present in a container or iterable.
core-syntax.identity: Check whether two references point to the exact same object; commonly used with None.
core-syntax.walrus: Assign a value inside a larger expression so the computed value can be reused immediately.
core-syntax.unpack: Take values from an iterable into separate names; a starred name collects the remaining values.
core-syntax.ignore value: Use _ by convention when a value is intentionally not needed.
core-syntax.delete: Remove a name, item, slice, or attribute binding; it does not necessarily destroy the underlying object.
core-syntax.docstring: Attach documentation text to a module, class, function, or method.
core-syntax.numeric separators: Use underscores to make long numeric literals easier to read without changing their value.

control-flow.if / elif / else: Run one branch based on conditions evaluated from top to bottom.
control-flow.ternary: Choose one of two values inside a single expression.
control-flow.for: Take values from an iterable one at a time and execute the loop body for each value.
control-flow.while: Repeat the loop body while a condition remains truthy.
control-flow.break: Exit the nearest loop immediately and continue after that loop.
control-flow.continue: Skip the rest of the current loop iteration and move to the next one.
control-flow.enumerate: Iterate over values while also receiving a counter, usually starting at zero.
control-flow.zip: Iterate over multiple iterables in parallel, producing tuples of corresponding items.
control-flow.for ... else: Run the else block only when the loop finishes normally rather than through break.
control-flow.while ... else: Run the else block only when the condition becomes false rather than the loop ending through break.
control-flow.match: Select a branch by structural pattern matching instead of a long chain of comparisons.
control-flow.match guard: Add an extra boolean condition to a structural pattern.
control-flow.wildcard case: Match any value not handled by an earlier case.

collections.list: Ordered, mutable sequence. Items can be replaced, added, removed, and reordered in place.
collections.tuple: Ordered, immutable sequence. The tuple cannot replace its items after creation.
collections.set: Mutable collection of unique hashable values with fast membership checks.
collections.dict: Mutable mapping from unique hashable keys to values.
collections.append / extend: Append adds one item; extend adds every item from another iterable.
collections.sort: Sort a list in place, or use sorted() to produce a new sorted list from any iterable.
collections.frozenset: Immutable set that can itself be used where a hashable value is required.
collections.copy: Create a shallow copy of the outer collection; nested objects remain shared.

functions.define: Create a reusable callable and bind it to a name.
functions.default arg: Use a fallback value when the caller omits that argument; avoid mutable objects as defaults.
functions.*args: Collect extra positional arguments into a tuple.
functions.**kwargs: Collect extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.
functions.keyword-only: Require arguments after * to be passed by name, improving call-site clarity.
functions.positional-only: Require arguments before / to be supplied by position rather than keyword.
functions.unpack call: Expand an iterable into positional arguments and a mapping into keyword arguments at the call site.
functions.lambda: Create a small anonymous single-expression function, often used as a key or callback.
functions.annotation: Describe the intended parameter and return types without changing normal runtime behavior by itself.
functions.multiple return: Return one tuple containing multiple values, which callers can unpack into separate names.
functions.LEGB: Python resolves a name through Local, Enclosing, Global, then Builtins scopes.
functions.global: Rebind a module-level name from inside a function.
functions.nonlocal: Rebind a name from the nearest enclosing function scope.
functions.first-class function: Functions are objects: they can be stored, passed to other functions, and returned.

iterators-generators.iterator: Stateful object that produces one value at a time through next() until it is exhausted.
iterators-generators.next: Ask an iterator for its next value; StopIteration signals that no values remain.
iterators-generators.generator: A function containing yield; calling it creates a lazy iterator and suspends state between yielded values.
iterators-generators.yield from: Delegate part of a generator to another iterable or generator.
iterators-generators.generator expr: Create a lazy iterator with comprehension-like syntax instead of constructing a full list.
iterators-generators.chain: Treat several iterables as one continuous sequence without copying their contents.
iterators-generators.islice: Take a slice-like window from an iterator without first turning it into a list.
iterators-generators.count / cycle: Produce an unbounded counter or repeatedly cycle through an iterable; consumers must decide when to stop.
iterators-generators.tee: Create independent iterator views backed by buffered values; heavy imbalance between them can consume memory.
iterators-generators.generator send: Resume a generator while injecting a value into the suspended yield expression.
iterators-generators.close: Stop a generator early by raising GeneratorExit inside it.

exceptions.try / except: Run code that may fail and handle a specific expected exception instead of crashing that control path.
exceptions.multiple types: Handle several related exception types with the same recovery logic.
exceptions.else: Run code only when the try block completed without an exception.
exceptions.finally: Run cleanup code whether the try block succeeds, fails, returns, or breaks out.
exceptions.raise: Create or propagate an exception deliberately when the current operation cannot continue correctly.
exceptions.re-raise: After logging or partial handling, propagate the currently handled exception unchanged.
exceptions.cause: Preserve an underlying exception as the explicit cause of a higher-level domain exception.
exceptions.custom error: Create an exception type that communicates a failure meaningful to your own domain.
exceptions.suppress: Intentionally ignore only named exception types inside a small, explicit block.
exceptions.ExceptionGroup: Carry several unrelated exceptions together, commonly from concurrent work.
exceptions.except*: Handle matching exceptions inside an ExceptionGroup while leaving unmatched ones to propagate.
exceptions.cleanup: Prefer context managers for resource cleanup because they encode enter/exit behavior reliably.

oop.class: Define a blueprint/type that describes attributes and behavior shared by its instances.
oop.constructor: Initialize a newly created instance; self is the instance being initialized.
oop.instance method: Method whose first parameter is the instance, conventionally named self.
oop.inheritance: Create a class that derives behavior from a base class and can extend or override it.
oop.super: Call behavior from the next class in the method-resolution order, usually a base implementation.
oop.property: Expose method-backed behavior using attribute syntax, optionally controlling reads and writes.
oop.class method: Method receiving the class as cls; useful for alternate constructors and class-level behavior.
oop.static method: Function namespaced inside a class that receives neither the instance nor class automatically.
oop.isinstance: Check whether an object is an instance of a class or its subclasses.
oop.issubclass: Check whether one class inherits from another.
oop.MRO: Show the order Python uses when looking up methods across inheritance hierarchies.
oop.composition: Build an object from other collaborating objects instead of inheriting all behavior.

typing.union: Allow a value to have any one of several declared types.
typing.optional: Allow either the declared value type or None.
typing.Callable: Describe a callable's parameter types and return type.
typing.Literal: Restrict a value to specific literal choices for static analysis.
typing.type alias: Give a reusable name to a type expression so complex annotations remain readable.
typing.Protocol: Describe behavior structurally: a value matches if it provides the required members.
typing.TypedDict: Describe the expected keys and value types of dictionary-shaped data.
typing.cast: Tell a type checker to treat a value as a type; it does not convert the runtime object.

modules-imports.import: Load a module and bind its module object to a name.
modules-imports.from import: Bind selected public objects from another module directly in the current namespace.
modules-imports.relative import: Import from the current package using dots to express package-relative location.
modules-imports.main guard: Run code only when this file is executed as the entry module, not when it is imported.
modules-imports.public API: Declare which names are exported by wildcard import and document the intended module surface.
modules-imports.run module: Execute a module through Python's module loader, preserving package import behavior.

files-pathlib.open safely: Use a context manager so the file is closed even if an exception occurs.
files-pathlib.binary mode: Read raw bytes rather than decoded text.
files-pathlib.join path: Combine path components using Path semantics instead of manual string separators.
files-pathlib.glob: Find paths whose names match a pattern; rglob searches recursively.
files-pathlib.resolve: Produce an absolute normalized path, resolving symlinks where the platform supports it.

concurrency.async function: Define a coroutine function. Calling it creates a coroutine object that must be awaited or scheduled.
concurrency.await: Pause the current coroutine until another awaitable completes, allowing the event loop to run other work.
concurrency.run event loop: Create an event loop, run the top-level coroutine, then cleanly shut the loop down.
concurrency.create task: Schedule a coroutine to run concurrently on the current event loop.
concurrency.gather: Await several awaitables and collect their results in input order.
concurrency.TaskGroup: Run related async tasks as one structured unit and propagate failures as a group.
concurrency.thread pool: Use operating-system threads, typically for blocking I/O or code that releases the GIL.
concurrency.process pool: Use separate processes for CPU-heavy Python work that benefits from true parallel execution.
concurrency.timeout: Limit how long an async block is allowed to wait before cancellation is triggered.
concurrency.sleep: Suspend a coroutine without blocking the event loop.
concurrency.queue: Coordinate producers and consumers without manually sharing a plain list.
concurrency.lock: Ensure only one coroutine at a time enters a protected async critical section.
concurrency.to_thread: Move a blocking synchronous function to a worker thread while keeping an async API.

testing.assert: Fail the current test when the expected condition is false.
testing.mock: Create a controllable test double that records calls and can return configured values.
testing.patch: Temporarily replace the name used by code under test, then restore it automatically.
testing.pytest fixture: Provide reusable setup/data to tests through dependency injection by parameter name.
testing.pytest raises: Assert that a block fails with an expected exception type.
testing.parametrize: Run one test function repeatedly with different input/expected-value combinations.
testing.monkeypatch: Temporarily modify environment variables, attributes, dictionaries, or paths for a test.
testing.tmp_path: Receive a unique temporary Path directory that pytest cleans up after the test session.

internals-gotchas.mutable default: A mutable default is created once when the function is defined, so later calls can unexpectedly share state.
internals-gotchas.late binding: Closures normally look up captured names when called, not when the closure was created.
internals-gotchas.identity vs equality: Identity asks 'same object?'; equality asks 'equivalent value?'. They answer different questions.
internals-gotchas.shallow copy: Copy only the outer object; references to nested objects remain shared.
internals-gotchas.deep copy: Recursively copy nested state to reduce sharing, which can be expensive or inappropriate for resource objects.
internals-gotchas.truthiness: Any value can participate in a condition; Python converts it through its truth-value rules.
internals-gotchas.hashability: Hashable objects have stable hashing/equality behavior and can be dictionary keys or set members.
internals-gotchas.iterator exhaustion: Most iterators are one-pass; once consumed, asking for more values does not restart them.
internals-gotchas.aliasing: Assignment can give one object several names, so mutation through one name is visible through the others.
internals-gotchas.sort return: In-place list methods generally return None to make mutation explicit rather than look like a new value.
internals-gotchas.EAFP: Perform the operation and handle the specific expected exception when failure is a normal possibility.
internals-gotchas.LBYL: Check a condition before acting when the check itself is meaningful, cheaper, or required.

theoryCards.title: Mutability & References
theoryCards.summary: The key mental model: variables are names bound to objects. Mutation changes an object; assignment changes what a name points to.

entries.meaning: The object can change in place, so every reference to that same object observes the change.
entries.detail: list · dict · set · most class instances

entries.meaning: The object itself cannot change in place; an apparent update creates another value and rebinds a name.
entries.detail: int · float · bool · str · tuple · frozenset · bytes

entries.meaning: Assignment points a name at an object. It does not clone the object.
Two names can refer to the same mutable object, so mutation through one name is visible through the other.
entries.detail: b = a · b.append(1) · a also changed

entries.meaning: Rebinding changes which object a name refers to; mutation changes the existing object itself.
Parameters are new local names bound to the caller's objects; mutating a passed mutable object can affect caller-visible state.
Create a new outer container while keeping references to the same nested objects.
Recursively copy nested state when the new structure really must be independent.

more.meaning: A tuple cannot replace its own elements, but an element may itself be a mutable object that can still change.
+= may mutate a mutable object such as a list, while immutable values such as strings produce a new object.
Function default objects are created once, so a mutable default can leak state between calls.
more.detail: def f(items=None): items = [] if items is None else items

more.meaning: For known simple shapes, copy the levels you need instead of automatically deep-copying everything.
id() identifies an object for its lifetime in the current process; it is useful for understanding aliasing, not business identity.

theoryCards.title: Identity, Hashing & Truthiness
theoryCards.summary: Three related rules decide how values compare, whether they can be keys, and how they behave inside conditions.

entries.meaning: Compare values using equality semantics, which classes can customize with __eq__.
Check whether both references point to the exact same object. Prefer it for None and unique sentinels.
A value has stable hash/equality behavior and may be used as a dictionary key or set member.
entries.detail: str · int · frozenset · tuple of hashable values

entries.meaning: Common mutable containers are deliberately unhashable because changing them would break hash-based lookup.
Conditions ask for a value's truth value; values are not required to literally be True or False.
None, false booleans, numeric zero, and empty containers/text evaluate as false.
Boolean operators short-circuit and return one of their operands, which makes fallback expressions possible.
Convert a value to its truth value and negate it, producing a real bool.

more.meaning: A class can define __bool__, or fall back to __len__, to control whether its instances are truthy.
Objects that compare equal must produce the same hash; mutable equality state therefore makes unsafe keys.
Use a unique object when None is a valid input and you need to distinguish 'missing' from 'explicitly None'.
Python can express range-style comparisons directly without repeating the middle operand.
Membership usually uses container-specific lookup or equality semantics, not object identity.
